title: Exercise-Associated Hyponatremia: 2017 Update
authors: Hew-Butler T, Loi V, Pani A, Rosner MH
population: Endurance and ultra-endurance athletes; review of EAH epidemiology, pathophysiology, treatment and prevention (follows the 2015 consensus)
findings: Overdrinking beyond thirst and non-osmotic arginine vasopressin release are the most common etiologic factors; a volume- and sodium-depletion contribution in a subset of athletes is also described (abstract).

Hyponatremia is blood [Na+] below 135 mmol/L; screening studies found asymptomatic EAH in 11% of 1,089 Ironman triathletes tested post-race and 67% of 15 ultramarathon runners tested during the race (full text).

Sodium ingestion cannot prevent EAH with excessive fluid intake; the amount of fluid ingested rather than sodium ingested drives final blood sodium, and hypotonic sodium-containing sports drinks will not prevent EAH in athletes who overdrink (full text).

Prevention: fixed fluid ranges are not appropriate; drinking when thirsty is the most individualized strategy; fluid deficits up to ~3% of body mass (~5% TBW) are well tolerated; thirst-guided drinking prevents EAH in temperate climates with duration under 17 h (full text).

Treatment: IV 100 mL 3% NaCl boluses every 10 min for severe symptomatic EAH, oral hypertonic solution for mild-moderate symptoms; 85% of hyponatremic athletes in one Czech ultra-endurance study were volume depleted by body-weight change, so weight loss does not exclude EAH (full text).
limitations: Narrative review, not a systematic search. Authors state that the evidence on sodium supplementation is mixed. The 17 h thirst-guided claim is for temperate climates and is an expert statement, not a tested threshold.
implications: Do not generate rigid fluid prescriptions above thirst; present fluid as a range (Tiller 450-750 mL/h) with a 'drink to thirst, do not force fluids' rule.
For events over ~17 h or hot races add a plan note: weigh at aid stations if possible, weight gain is a red flag, avoid water-only/hypotonic overdrinking.
Frame sodium as secondary to avoiding overdrinking.
Include a safety card with EAH warning symptoms and a medical-care directive; no treatment prescription in the engine.

verification.notes: Crossref match. Abstract from Europe PMC. Full text (PMC5334560) re-fetched as XML and searched directly: 1,089 Ironman, 67% of 15 ultramarathoners, 135 mmol/L, 100 mL 3% saline every 10 min, 17 h, 3% body mass and Czech 85% all confirmed verbatim.
